extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance to young people who wish to become authors, covering how to organize life and motives, how to research and write political and literary prose, and what professions or habits best sustain serious literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Impartiality means 'an honest and enlightened adherence to a code of intelligible principles previously announced, and faithfully referred to in support of every judgment on men and events'; not indiscriminate abuse, not the indulgence of an editor's own malignant passions, and not pandering to 'the envy and cupidity... of the half-witted vulgar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A newspaper that combines genuine impartiality with respectable literary talent will succeed without party patronage; impartiality requires publicly-stated principles consistently applied in judgments and criticism rather than opportunistic flattery or malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place events in a moral point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the questions and events of the day 'in a moral point of view'; give dignity to particular measures by tracing their policy or impolicy to permanent principles, and give interest to principles by their application to individual measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political essays should connect contemporary actions to enduring moral or political principles so that measures are judged by consistent standards rather than transient party feeling; this method increases the lasting value of journalistic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-comparative method for political writing
rubrics_metrics.description: On every great occurrence, endeavour to discover in past history the event that most nearly resembled it; procure contemporary historians, memorialists, and pamphleteers; subtract the points of difference from those of likeness and then conjecture whether the result will be the same or different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful comparison with well-chosen historical parallels (examples: comparing France under Napoleon with Rome under the early Caesars, or the Spanish revolution with the war of the United Provinces under Philip II) and base judgments on primary and contemporary sources to strengthen political argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define political terms precisely (rescue words from abuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly define and analyse political terms (example given: Jacobinism), distinguishing them from related but different categories (republican, democrat, demagogue) to prevent the term remaining a mere term of abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying definitions protects honest minds from adopting mistaken conclusions and allows more precise critique; making such distinctions is both an intellectual and ethical service in political writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use primary documents and authentic contemporary accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Arm yourself with 'the original documents of the past, together with authentic accounts of the present' when judging or predicting national events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on primary sources and trustworthy contemporary reportage rather than secondary compilations; original documents enable more accurate analogies and predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop philosophic tact for salient facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a 'philosophic tact for what is truly important in facts' and in most instances select facts that modern historians have excluded from their volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate judgment to recognize which particulars really matter to argument and which are mere noise; privileging the right facts strengthens historical and political analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never pursue literature as a trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Never pursue literature as a trade; making literature into mere dependence on immediate returns converts the stimulant of motive into a 'narcolic' and stuns the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat literary work as vocation or calling rather than as an income-focused profession; excessive preoccupation with money or immediate reputation blunts genius and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain regular non-literary employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep 'some regular employment, which does not depend on the will of the moment' — employment that can be carried on mechanically so that three hours of leisure, unannoyed, will suffice to realize a larger product of genial work than weeks of compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A steady day occupation (law, manufacturing, medicine, etc.) supplies stability, relieves the pressure for immediate output, and makes the leisure devoted to literature more productive; historical examples given: Cicero, Xenophon, Sir Thomas More, Bacon, Darwin, Roscoe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide talents and genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Devote talents to the acquirement of competence in some known trade or profession, and devote genius to objects of tranquil and unbiassed choice; the consciousness of both being equally a duty will ennoble both pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical competence secures material independence and frames the conditions in which genius can act freely; this split preserves creative freedom while ensuring livelihood and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid money and immediate reputation as primary motivators
rubrics_metrics.description: Money and immediate reputation 'form only an arbitrary and accidental end of literary labor' and the necessity of acquiring them often converts a stimulant into a narcotic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let the desire for pay or fame dominate literary effort; excessive motive reverses itself and dulls creative energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a scholar's utility by truths diffused, not publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The criterion of a scholar's utility should be 'the number and moral value of the truths which he has been the means of throwing into the general circulation,' or the influence on conversation and letters, not merely how many books or publications he produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure impact by the value and spread of ideas and influence on others (lectures, conversations, republications) rather than raw bibliographic output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate self-control and concentrate powers for permanent work
rubrics_metrics.description: Lament the deficiency in self-control that prevents concentrating powers to realize some permanent work; the neglect of concentrating gifts leads to a sense of wasted prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to focus energies toward enduring projects rather than frittering talents on ephemeral pieces; self-discipline is essential to produce lasting literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine literary pursuits with active social life
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits of active life and daily intercourse with the world give self-command so that family presence need not interrupt study; social silence or the undisturbing voices of family may act as a restorative atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engagement with society and family can refresh the mind and provide material and restraint for literary work; seclusion is not the only route to creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a profession that supports scholarly pursuits (e.g., the clergy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church (clergy) offers a profession where learning and genius may unite with professional duties; the clergyman is both neighbor and family-man, with access to both rich and poor, and the office provides patronage encouraging learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select occupations whose decorum, duties, and position provide both time and social role conducive to serious literary study and the diffusion of moral and critical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering, malignancy, and mob-sycophancy in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not indulge an editor's malignant passions nor adopt 'a determination to make money by flattering the envy and cupidity, the vindictive restlessness and self-conceit of the half-witted vulgar' — a behavior boasted of by 'mob-sycophants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist sensationalism and pandering to base popular instincts; such conduct is morally wrong and degrades the writer's work and the public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that complexity of prose invites criticism but may indicate seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose may be charged with 'a disproportionate demand on the attention; with an excess of refinement... with the length and laborious construction of periods; in short with obscurity and the love of paradox.' Yet such complexity is not the same as triviality or tricking out others' thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be conscious that refined, difficult, or paradoxical prose will attract critical charges; weigh clarity against depth but recognize that substantial thinking often requires laborious form; avoid mere obscurity that disguises emptiness.
